title: CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) over TCP, TLS, and WebSockets
summary: CoAP was designed to run over UDP, but some environments do better with reliable transports. This document defines how to carry CoAP over TCP, TLS and WebSockets, including changes to the message format and how connections are managed.

eli5.summary: A tiny-device messaging system normally sends loose notes. This lets it use sturdier connections that make sure the notes arrive.

questions: how does coap framing work over tcp
what is a coap csm message
subtitle: How CoAP, built for UDP, is carried over TCP, TLS and WebSockets, with a new framing and signaling messages.

tldr.problem: CoAP was designed for UDP, but some networks do not forward UDP packets, and some deployments, such as browser-based applications, can only use TCP-based connections.
tldr.mechanism: CoAP messages drop the Type, Message ID and Version fields and gain a length field. Reliability comes from the transport, and a new class of signaling messages (CSM, Ping, Pong, Release, Abort) manages the connection.
tldr.outcome: CoAP can run over TCP, TLS and WebSockets, with four new URI schemes and a block-wise extension for larger messages. RFC 8974 later updated this document.

today: RFC 8323 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7641 and RFC 7959, and it has itself been updated by RFC 8974. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why CoAP Needs Reliable Transports
sections.content:
The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP, RFC 7252) was designed for Internet of Things deployments on UDP, with a low code footprint and small messages. The main reason to carry it over TCP and TLS is that some networks do not forward UDP. The RFC cites complete UDP blocking in between about 2% and 4% of terrestrial access networks, concentrated in enterprise networks and regions with challenged connectivity.

TCP also changes NAT behavior. NATs often keep TCP bindings longer than UDP ones, so fewer keepalive messages are needed. The RFC quotes a mean binding timeout of 386 minutes for TCP and 160 seconds for UDP. TCP's congestion and flow control also help with larger payloads. Another case is CoAP applications inside a web browser, where WebSockets can carry CoAP without translating it to HTTP.

The RFC is clear that CoAP over UDP (and over DTLS) is still the recommended transport in constrained node networks. CoAP over TCP is for cases where the network leaves no other choice, because it costs more code size, round trips, RAM and packet size. The document also formally updates RFC 7641 (Observe) and RFC 7959 (block-wise transfer) for reliable transports.
sections.eli5: Some buildings block the quick-note way of sending messages. This gives the gadgets another route that is slower to set up but reliably gets through.

sections.title: The Length-Prefixed Message Format
sections.content:
Over UDP, each datagram keeps messages apart and gives their length. A byte stream does not, so CoAP over TCP needs a length field. Because TCP already retransmits and removes duplicates, the Type and Message ID fields are removed. The Version field is also removed, since CoAP is version 1 and there is no known reason for another. Capabilities and Settings Messages were designed so version negotiation could be added later if needed.

The first byte holds a 4-bit Len and a 4-bit token length (TKL). A value from 0 to 12 is the length in bytes of everything from the start of the Options field to the end of the payload. The values 13, 14 and 15 mean an 8-bit, 16-bit or 32-bit Extended Length follows, and the length is that number plus 13, 269 or 65805 respectively. The Code, token, options and payload follow as in RFC 7252.

As an example, a message with just code 2.03 and Token 7f is encoded in three bytes: 0x01 0x43 0x7f.
sections.eli5: On a long stream of bytes, you need to say how long each message is, like writing the length on the front of each parcel so the receiver knows where one ends and the next begins.

sections.title: Connections and Signaling Messages
sections.content:
Once a connection is open, each side MUST send a Capabilities and Settings Message (CSM, code 7.01) as its first message. It carries things such as the maximum message size or support for block-wise transfer. The connection initiator must not wait for the acceptor's CSM before sending its own, but the acceptor may wait. A missing or invalid CSM is a connection error. The Max-Message-Size option has a base value of 1152 bytes.

Requests and responses are asynchronous. A client can send several requests without waiting, responses can come in any order and must use the same connection, and Tokens, scoped to the connection, tell requests apart. Either side may send requests, since the connection is bidirectional.

Signaling is a third kind of message, after requests and responses, using codes 7.00 to 7.31. Besides CSM, the document defines Ping (7.02) and Pong (7.03), where the receiver MUST answer a Ping with a Pong carrying the same Token. A Custody option can ask the receiver to delay its Pong until earlier messages are processed. A Release message (7.04) asks the peer to close the connection in an orderly way, and can carry an Alternative-Address or a Hold-Off option. An Abort message (7.05) means the sender cannot continue and closes the connection straight away. Empty messages (code 0.00) are ignored and serve as a basic keepalive.
sections.eli5: When two devices connect, they first swap a short note about what they can handle. After that, they can send a quick 'are you there?' and get an answer, or politely say goodbye, or hang up in a hurry if something is wrong.

sections.title: CoAP over WebSockets
sections.content:
CoAP over WebSockets is intentionally similar to CoAP over TCP, so the RFC only lists the differences. The client opens a WebSocket connection as defined in RFC 6455, and MUST include the subprotocol name coap in the handshake. The Host header also sets the default value of the Uri-Host option.

CoAP messages travel as binary WebSocket frames. The format is the same as for TCP except that Len MUST be zero, since the WebSocket frame already carries the length. WebSockets give retransmission and deduplication, so there is no distinction between confirmable and non-confirmable messages. The WebSocket Ping and unsolicited Pong frames SHOULD NOT be used, because CoAP Ping and Pong already do the job.

The RFC shows three setups: a client talking directly to a WebSocket server that hosts CoAP, a client using a WebSocket-to-UDP CoAP proxy, and a CoAP server inside a web browser that is reached through a reverse proxy.
sections.eli5: Web pages can only use certain roads. WebSockets is one of those roads, so CoAP just rides along on it with a few small changes.

sections.title: Block-Wise Transfer and Observing
sections.content:
Over reliable transports the message size limits that avoid IP fragmentation are no longer needed, but block-wise transfer (RFC 7959) still helps. Large messages such as firmware downloads can cause head-of-line blocking on a single connection, and a UDP-to-TCP gateway may not be able to convert a block-wise exchange into one exchange. The RFC adds BERT (Block-wise Extension for Reliable Transport): a Block1 or Block2 option with the size field SZX equal to 7. A BERT block payload is a multiple of 1024 bytes, so one message can carry several blocks. Support is announced with the Block-Wise-Transfer option together with a Max-Message-Size above 1152.

Observing resources (RFC 7641) is adjusted too. Notification sequence numbers are not needed because delivery is ordered, so the Observe value MAY be empty and MUST be ignored on reception. Confirmable and non-confirmable notifications do not exist. A client cannot cancel by answering with a Reset, so it MUST deregister with a GET carrying the observation's Token and Observe value 1. When the connection closes or times out, the server removes the client's observations. One CoAP Ping can check the connection and all its observations at once.
sections.eli5: Sending a huge file in one go can hog the pipe, so it is cut into pieces. This update lets several pieces ride together in one message, like loading a few boxes on one truck.

sections.title: New URI Schemes and Ports
sections.content:
Four new URI schemes name CoAP resources by transport: coap+tcp, coaps+tcp (TCP secured by TLS), coap+ws and coaps+ws (WebSockets, secured by TLS in the second). Resources under different schemes have no shared identity, even for the same host and port.

The default port is 5683 for coap+tcp and 5684 for coaps+tcp. For other TLS ports, the client MUST use the ALPN extension to offer the coap protocol identifier. The coap+ws scheme defaults to port 80 and coaps+ws to port 443. Their WebSocket endpoint is the authority of the URI plus the well-known path /.well-known/coap, and the remaining path and query identify the CoAP resource, for example coap+ws://example.org/sensors/temperature?u=Cel.

Default Uri-Host and Uri-Port values come from the destination address and TCP port, from the SNI host when SNI is used with TLS, or from the Host header in a WebSocket handshake.
sections.eli5: Each way of reaching a gadget gets its own web-address style prefix, so you can tell from the address whether it uses the plain pipe, the locked pipe, or the web pipe.

sections.title: Securing CoAP over Reliable Transports
sections.content:
A security solution MUST be implemented for CoAP over reliable transports and MUST be enabled by default. The document defines a TLS binding but allows other layers to be used. For TCP, the TLS guidance in RFC 7925 applies. A device ends up in one of four modes: NoSec (TLS disabled and optional to implement), PreSharedKey, RawPublicKey or Certificate. One of the last three is mandatory to implement, depending on the credential type. Less constrained devices should follow RFC 7525 instead, and an implementation that must support both cases follows both.

For coaps+ws, the client MUST perform a TLS handshake after opening the connection. WebSocket servers serving browsers MUST follow RFC 7525.

The security considerations of RFC 7252 apply, and so do those of RFC 6455 for WebSockets. For signaling, the Alternative-Address option cannot be followed blindly: a peer MUST NOT assume a connection to the alternative address inherits the security properties of the current one.
sections.eli5: Locks must be built in and turned on by default. Even if a message tells you to go to a new address, do not assume it is as safe as the old one.

items.label: CSM
items.desc: Capabilities and settings, sent first by each endpoint.

items.label: Ping
items.desc: Tests the connection; the peer must reply with a Pong.

items.label: Pong
items.desc: Reply to a Ping with the same Token.

items.label: Release
items.desc: Asks the peer to close the connection in an orderly way.

items.label: Abort
items.desc: The sender cannot continue and shuts the connection immediately.
